mainEntity.name: How much does a BMW 5 Series 518d engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A BMW 5 Series 518d engine replacement typically costs between £1,500 and £5,800 for the engine itself, depending on condition. Used engines start from around £1,200-£1,500, while reconditioned and rebuilt units range from £2,800 to £5,800. Supply and fitting adds approximately £650-£910 in labour for an indie specialist, or more at a main dealer.

mainEntity.name: What are the signs of timing chain failure in a BMW 5 Series 518d?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most common warning sign is a rattling or metallic noise from the engine on cold start, lasting a few seconds. Other symptoms include rough idling, reduced performance, and engine warning lights. If the chain snaps, the engine will fail catastrophically - valves and pistons can collide, requiring a full engine replacement.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in a BMW 5 Series 518d?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the vehicle's value and the extent of the damage. For an F10-generation 518d worth £4,000-£8,000, a full rebuilt engine at £3,800-£5,800 may represent 50-80% of the car's value - a used engine or repair may be more sensible. For a G30-generation 518d worth £12,000-£25,000, a rebuilt engine is a financially sound investment.

mainEntity.name: How long does a BMW 5 Series 518d engine replacement take?

acceptedAnswer.text: A full BMW 5 Series 518d engine replacement typically takes between 5 and 10 working days, depending on the internal condition found during stripdown and parts availability. Supply-only options can be dispatched within 1-2 working days, with fitting then scheduled at your chosen specialist.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between the BMW 518d and 520d engine?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both the 518d and 520d use the same 2.0-litre four-cylinder diesel engine family (N47 or B47), but with different power outputs. The 518d produces 143-150bhp, while the 520d produces 184-190bhp. The engines are physically similar, but the 520d uses a different turbocharger and engine calibration to achieve higher power.

mainEntity.name: Can I replace my N47 engine with a B47 in my BMW 5 Series 518d?

acceptedAnswer.text: While both engines are 2.0-litre diesels and share the same mounting points, an N47-to-B47 swap is not a straightforward bolt-in replacement. The B47 uses different engine management, wiring looms, sensors, and emissions systems (including AdBlue on later models). A full conversion requires extensive electrical work and is rarely cost-effective compared to fitting the correct engine for your chassis.

historyTimeline.h2: BMW 5 Series 518d - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The BMW 518d was introduced in 2013 as the entry-level diesel in the F10 5 Series range, offering a fuel-efficient 2.0-litre four-cylinder diesel that made executive motoring more accessible. Over its production life, the 518d evolved from the N47 to the B47 engine family, bringing improved reliability and emissions compliance.

milestones.description: N47D20C (N47T), 2.0L diesel, 143bhp - launch engine for the F10/F11 518d
B47D20A, 2.0L diesel, 150bhp - facelift introduction of the modular B47 engine family
B47D20B, 2.0L diesel, 150bhp - G30/G31 generation 518d with updated calibration
B47D20B with mild-hybrid, 2.0L diesel, 150bhp - 48V mild-hybrid system added

commonProblems.h2: BMW 5 Series 518d Engine Problems - Repair Cost vs Replacement
commonProblems.h3: The BMW 5 Series 518d is powered by two generations of 2.0-litre diesel - the earlier N47D20C and the later B47D20A/B. While the B47 addressed many of the N47's weaknesses, the rear-mounted timing chain on N47-equipped 518d models remains a significant concern. Rebuilt engines supplied through EnginesMarket include upgraded components addressing the original failure point, plus a minimum 12-month unlimited-mileage warranty.

problems.h4: Timing Chain Failure - Why the BMW 5 Series 518d N47 Engine Wears Prematurely
problems.rootCause: The timing chain is located at the rear of the engine, and the tensioner can fail to apply proper tension, causing the chain to stretch. Early warning signs include a rattling noise on cold start.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace chain, tensioner, guides; rear-chain access requires gearbox removal
repairOptions.longevity: Viable if caught early before engine damage

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit, upgraded components addressing the original failure point, 12-month warranty
repairOptions.longevity: Best if chain has already failed or engine has sustained damage

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical BMW 5 Series 518d (F10, 2013-2016) is worth approximately £4,000-£12,000 depending on mileage and condition. A full rebuilt engine at £3,800-£5,800 represents 30-60% of the vehicle's value - on lower-value examples (sub-£5,000), a used engine or timing chain repair may be more financially sensible.
problems.recommendation: If you catch the timing chain rattle early, the chain replacement route (around £1,200-£2,200 at a specialist) is the most cost-effective option. If the chain has already snapped or caused valve/piston damage, a full rebuilt engine with upgraded components and warranty is the safer long-term bet.
problems.cta: -> Compare rebuilt N47D20C BMW 5 Series 518d engine prices

problems.h4: EGR Cooler Failure - B47 Engine Weakness
problems.rootCause: The EGR cooler can develop internal coolant leaks, allowing coolant to enter the exhaust system. This can cause white smoke, loss of coolant, and in extreme cases, a fire risk. BMW issued a recall for this issue.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace EGR cooler and associated seals

repairOptions.longevity: Only if engine damage has occurred

problems.vehicleValueCheck: For a typical BMW 5 Series 518d (G30, 2018-present) worth £12,000-£25,000, the £600-£1,200 EGR cooler repair is well within the vehicle's value and the obvious choice. Replacement is only warranted if the failure has caused secondary engine damage.
problems.recommendation: EGR cooler failure is a well-documented issue with a straightforward fix. Address it promptly at a specialist - the repair cost is modest relative to the value of the car, and ignoring it can lead to far more expensive consequences.
